examples: Jeremiah's statement is conditional: “If I say…” The question turns it into an actual attempt by saying, “When Jeremiah tries to stop speaking…” Keep the condition rather than asserting that Jeremiah tried to stop.

“Those cities” points back to the preceding card and has no antecedent within this question. The question needs to identify them as the cities Jeremiah wants the man who brought the birth news to be like.
The opening word "THREE" calls back to the three cities in verse 2, but the card cites only verse 3. Because this story card uses both verses, its citation should be Deuteronomy 19:2-3.

Verse 9 commands Israel to add three more cities, but the walkthrough only says "more cities" and never supplies the number. The baker therefore misses a central detail of Moses' instruction about the additional cities.

The card describes the false witness being exposed as a liar who falsely accused his brother, the serious sin this passage calls evil, and then adds a cookie joke. This heavy moment should remain joke-free.
This is the stop's second drawer-years joke; card 3 already jokes about telling time by dust in the drawer.
The wrong answer 'Baked with honey' reuses card 4's wrong answer 'Bread baked with honey.' 'Baked without leaven' also restates card 4's correct answer, 'Unleavened bread.'
The card tells verse 24's trumpet blasts and verse 27's Day of Atonement, but nothing from verses 25 or 26. Its citation of Leviticus 23:24-27 is therefore wider than what it tells.

Papa Dorin adds new backstory by saying that the first thing he did with his freedom was fill cookie boxes. The established account has him renewed, speaking with the angel and making his two requests before any box-filling is described. Mentioning the drawer and cookie boxes is fine, but this invents a new first-action chronology.

The card asks the baker to supply the unseen wording at the end of Galatians 5:15. No story card develops this warning first, and "devouring" already supplies the idea behind "consumed," making this a prediction of the verse's next word rather than a reasoned question about its movement or meaning.

The apron punchline comes on a heavy card in the middle of the severe judgment prayer, asking for cursing to soak into the man's body and bones. Making the joke self-deprecating does not keep the heavy moment light; this card should carry no joke.

Card 7 has just quoted the older son saying “this son of yours,” which directly settles card 8's claim that he calls the younger son “my brother.” The preceding card gives away the False answer instead of leaving a new detail for the baker to work out.

The blank asks for an unseen detail of the verse rather than a meaning the baker can reliably infer. Tying a donkey to a vine does not establish that garments are washed in wine; without already knowing the verse, the baker is largely guessing among the three liquids.

The setup does not give the baker a sufficient basis for distinguishing a wolf from an eagle or a bear. Devouring prey and dividing plunder leave the baker to recall or guess the unseen animal rather than reason out the answer from the earlier cards.

The question depends on the preceding story card for its context: both "also" and "that cave" point back to the burial-site card. Standing alone, it does not identify which burial cave Jacob is discussing.
The wrong answer "The priests" repeats the wrong answer "priests" from stop 3, card 4. Wrong answers, like right answers, must not be reused on later cards.
The question already names Jesus in "Jesus says" and "His name," while the correct answer is "Jesus Himself." The question therefore contains its own answer.

Too many choices require guessing an unrevealed detail rather than reasoning from the earlier cards. Cards 2, 5, 7, 10, 11, 13 and 17 provide no basis for choosing among their options: the setup cards merely say that Jesus gives something, sends a message, gives packing instructions, gives lodging and rejection instructions, or that rumors circulate. Seven of the eleven choice cards thus function as discovery questions, so most of the stop's choices are not informed guesses.

The opening card never mentions what Jesus gives the Twelve, so the baker can only guess "demons" as the missing word from wording they have not seen. The blank does not test a meaning they can reason out.
The Twelve's departure in verse 6 is never set up on a story card. Card 12 is still telling verse 5, and the setup for this choice appears only inside its own question.
The card calls back to wisdom taking her stand at the crossroads in Proverbs 8:2, but it cites only Proverbs 8:36. The citation does not cover all the passage content the card uses.

The card explicitly calls back to what the psalmist did when the arrogant lied about him in verse 78, but it cites only verse 95. Since the card uses both verses, its citation should include Psalm 119:78 as well, such as Psalm 119:78, 95.
The card says Israel is out of Egypt, which uses verse 1, but it cites only verse 2. Its citation should cover Exodus 19:1-2.

Even apart from the fill-in-the-blank cards, cards 2, 5, 8, 10, 12 and 19 require details that earlier cards neither supply nor make inferable. Thus six of the stop's eight other choices are discoveries, leaving most of the stop's choices dependent on guessing rather than reasoning.

Six blanks ask for wording the baker has never seen and cannot infer: stop 1 cards 3, 7, 14 and 20, and stop 2 cards 8 and 18. Nothing in the earlier cards lets the baker reason out third, possession, clothes, ram's horn, furnace or Aaron.

The wrong answer "By staying silent" reuses the wrong-answer idea "A time to stay quiet" from stop 1, card 17. Both concern staying quiet in response to persecution, so rewording it does not make it a new answer.

Most choice cards are discovery questions rather than informed guesses. Stop 1 cards 2, 5, 6, 8 and 11, and stop 2 cards 2, 3 and 4, ask for facts that the earlier cards give no basis to infer. That makes eight of the eleven choices dependent on prior knowledge or luck, rather than only a few discovery questions.
Four of the stop's five choice cards are multiple choice, with only one true-or-false card and no fill-in-the-blank card. Multiple choice therefore dominates the stop by a wide margin.

The wrong answer 'That Aaron had died on Mount Hor' is true elsewhere in the passage: Numbers 33:38-39 says Aaron died on Mount Hor. A wrong answer cannot merely be false for this particular moment while being true elsewhere in the passage.

This card says "the evil treasure of his heart" immediately before card 18 asks for the missing word in "out of the overflow of the ___." It directly supplies "heart," the answer to that later choice.

Nothing in the earlier cards lets the baker reason that the light of David's eyes is what fades. The sound of his voice and the grip of his hands are equally plausible symptoms, so the baker can only guess an unseen detail of the psalm's wording.
The choice depends on knowing the hard word "iniquity" well enough to supply it as the correct answer. Understanding that difficult word should not be what determines whether the baker can answer.
The setup only says that Jesus makes something from cords. Nothing in the earlier cards lets the baker reason out "whip" rather than "sling" or "net," so this blank depends on luck.
Nothing in the earlier cards gives a basis for inferring forty-six years. The baker can only guess among the three numbers, rather than reason out the blank's meaning.

The preceding story card only covers Joseph's descendants, so nothing sets up the Levites' situation before this blank. The baker must supply the unseen word "cities" from three plausible kinds of dwellings, making this an unseen-word guess rather than a blank whose meaning can be reasoned out.
The statement combines two claims: Joshua turns Caleb down, and Joshua gives the hill country to another tribe. The true/false card should test only one claim about Joshua's response.

The earlier cards establish only the Pharisees' careful tithing; they give no basis for supplying the unseen word "justice." This blank asks for the next wording of Jesus' line rather than a meaning the baker can reason out.
The boss-at-4:59 comparison is a joke on the same card that says the experts' fathers killed the prophets.
Six of the eight choice cards are multiple choice, leaving only two true-or-false cards and no fill-in-the-blank cards. Multiple choice therefore dominates the stop by a wide margin.

The correct answer depends on understanding the unfamiliar expression "support in the gate," and the preceding story card gives no context for it. A baker who does not understand that expression cannot reason through the choice.

This story card has three full sentences: one about the disciples not being of the world, one about Jesus choosing them out of it, and one about Papa Dorin's clearance bin. The fragment "Me?" does not reduce that count.
"Moses" is used as a wrong answer here after already appearing as a wrong answer on card 2.

The question refers only to "all these things" without reestablishing that Jesus has been warning His disciples about hatred and persecution. With the story card no longer on screen, the question lacks the context needed to reason out why He gave the warning.
The blank asks for the exact fraction Zacchaeus gives, but the earlier cards provide no basis for choosing half rather than a tenth or all. A baker can only guess the amount.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the millstone warning, "This part is heavy.", and the sentence introducing "Watch yourselves." That exceeds the two-sentence limit.

The question already says that the servant "did what he was told," and the correct answer merely restates that as "The servant only did his job." The question therefore contains a form of its own answer.
The last six choice cards follow a repeated pattern: multiple choice on cards 5, 9 and 12, each followed by true or false on cards 7, 11 and 14.
The wrong answer 'He will send her back to Moab' reuses the return-to-Moab answer idea already shown as 'A way back to Moab' on stop 1, card 2.

The question begins “After hearing that,” but does not say what the woman heard. Its essential context is Jesus telling her about her five husbands and the man she now has, which appears only on the preceding story card that is no longer on screen.

The setup says only that one thing must never touch the Nazirite's head. It has not mentioned growing or cutting hair, so the baker cannot reason out "razor" rather than "comb" or "crown." The blank asks for wording and detail the baker has not seen.

Nothing in the earlier cards gives the baker a basis for working out when the day of cleansing comes. "Seventh," "third" and "tenth" are unsupported guesses, so this blank tests an unseen detail rather than a meaning the baker can reason out.

The card mentions atonement but leaves out verse 11's stated reason: the Nazirite has sinned by being in the presence of the dead body. No other card supplies this important explanation for the sin offering and atonement.
The earlier cards give no basis for choosing "serve" over "thank" or "follow." The blank asks for an unseen verb from verse 39 rather than a meaning the baker can reason out.
Nothing in the earlier cards identifies Jesus as the Christ or connects the demons' "Son of God" shout to that title. The baker can only guess the unseen word "Christ."
The card calls back to the crowds in verse 42 and to Jesus' good-news mission in verse 43, then tells verse 44, but its citation skips verse 43.
Four of the six choice cards (cards 5, 8, 9 and 11) are true or false, while the other two are multiple choice. True or false therefore dominates the stop by a wide margin.
The statement uses "it" for the Pharisee's thought without restating what that thought was. Since the preceding card is no longer on screen, the question does not supply its full context.

Luke 7:40 is the immediate lead-in to the parable: Jesus tells Simon that He has something to tell him, and Simon asks Him to speak. It is placed in stop 1, while the parable's stop begins at Luke 7:41; the lead-in should join stop 2.
The card places Job and his friends in a "room," but the passage gives no such setting. The silence can be described without adding a location.

The citation runs through verse 5, but the summary stops with Jair's sons and towns in verse 4. It never uses Jair's death and burial in Kamon from verse 5, so the citation is wider than what the card tells.
The card recounts Israel's corporate idolatry and forsaking of the LORD, then attaches the loyalty-card punchline. This is a joke on a card telling serious sin.
The card tells that the Ammonites are crossing the Jordan to fight Judah, Benjamin and Ephraim, then adds the work-and-doorbell punchline. The joke sits on a card telling violence.
The card repeats that the man was lame from birth, which comes from Acts 3:2, but cites only Acts 3:8. The citation should include both verses it uses: Acts 3:2, 8.
The card tells the crowd's turning back from Acts 3:19 as well as the results in Acts 3:20, but it cites only Acts 3:20. It should cite Acts 3:19-20.

This choice card asks about the violent act itself: the correct answer is that the tenants wounded the third servant and threw him out. The violence should be told on a story card, with any choice focusing on the choices or results around it.

The card retells the sending and rejection of all three servants from Luke 20:10-12 before moving to the owner's words in Luke 20:13, but it cites only Luke 20:13. Its citation should run from Luke 20:10 through Luke 20:13.

The blank asks for the new detail "Father," but no earlier card identifies who sent Jesus or gives the baker a basis for choosing Father over prophets or elders. This asks the baker to guess wording from a line they have not seen rather than reason out its meaning.

The preceding card does not establish whether the people can come where Jesus is going. All three words fit the sentence, so the baker can only guess the unseen word "cannot" from Jesus' next line rather than reason out the answer.

This non-opening story card has three full sentences: the retelling of verse 3, followed by “Tyre didn't go out shopping, friend.” and “The shopping sailed right up to HER.” Later story cards are limited to one or two sentences.

The correct answer, “There is no longer a harbor,” was already disclosed in stop 1 card 3's correct answer, “Tyre is laid waste with no house or harbor.” The later question therefore reuses an answer detail the baker has already seen rather than asking something new.

The card explicitly calls back to verse 1 with “that cry again” and “Same ships, same wailing,” while also telling verse 14. Its citation lists only Isaiah 23:14, omitting the earlier verse used in the callback.

Card 8 already asks about the first parallel line of Psalm 127:3, where children are a heritage from the LORD. This card then questions the second line, which makes the same point by calling the fruit of the womb His reward, rather than asking something new.

The line introduces Mags, who is not an established Dorinverse character or one of the six cookie-cutter kids, and gives her a new role in the Millers' kitchen. This adds a new named person and memory to Papa Dorin's story.
Papa Dorin names Chip only as "my Chip." He does not tell the baker that Chip is one of his cookie-cutter kids.

Discovery questions dominate the walkthrough instead of remaining a few exceptions. For example, stop 1 cards 2, 5, 7 and 9, and stop 2 cards 2, 5, 6 and 12 ask for details the earlier cards give no basis to reason out, leaving the baker largely to guess.
The card repeats the outside-passage fact from Luke 22:37 that Jesus said He would be numbered with the transgressors, but it does not give Luke 22:37 in brackets in the card's text.

Neither blank can be reasoned from the setup. A sword strike does not establish that the ear was cut off, and nothing makes "right" more inferable than "left," so this fill-in-the-blank tests an unseen detail by luck.
